title: Battles in the Supreme Court -- Ch. 6: BATTLES ON THE ECONOMIC FRONT
keywords: we do not administer justice by plebiscite
Iglesia ni Cristo v. Court of Appeals
right to strike of public schoolteachers
courts are the temples of right
primary_topics: Chapter 6 of 'Battles in the Supreme Court' -- CJP's account of the Court's most business-criticized ruling, Tatad v. Secretary of Energy, which invalidated RA 8180, the Oil Deregulation Law, by 9 to 2, and of his own effort to explain that ruling to the business community

His Concurring Opinion's central reframing: the issue is not whether the Court may fix oil prices or interfere in economics, but whether a law that lets the oil companies unilaterally set prices is constitutional -- and by annulling it the Court was not opposing deregulation but striking a 'pseudo-deregulation law' that perpetuated a cartel

The postscript speech he delivered to the Rotary Club of Makati on January 6, 1998, reproduced in full, answering five criticisms of the Decision and explaining the doctrine that the Court voids an economic measure only for unconstitutionality or grave abuse of discretion

His broader defense of judicial review over economic matters: the 1987 Charter uniquely enshrines economic rights, separation of powers is justified by checks and balances, and 'that justices are not economists or businessmen cannot lessen the cogency or binding effect of their decisions'
sub_topics: The ruling and its critics: through Justice Puno the Court invalidated RA 8180 by 9 to 2, and the 'Ayala Avenue critics' accused it of undue interference in economic matters said to be beyond its competence and authority

The Court's finding: RA 8180 let Petron, Shell and Caltex act as a monopoly or, more precisely, an oligopoly, acting in concert in their overt dealings with the public and particularly in price-fixing, offending the constitutional ban on monopolies and combinations in restraint of trade
Justice Puno's key line, that the Constitution mandates the Court to be the guardian not only of the people's political rights but of their economic rights as well

CJP's Concurring Opinion, point one: the Court has no desire and no power to change or repeal the laws of economics any more than those of physics or chemistry; the real issue is the validity of the law allowing unilateral pricing, and the Court has the duty, not just the power, to annul a law that offends the Constitution

The status quo order of October 7, 1997 directing the three oil companies to cease and desist from increasing prices for thirty days, issued after the petition, comments, reply and the September 30, 1997 oral argument showed the law prima facie constitutionally infirm

Point two of the concurrence: everyone, rich or poor, must share in the burdens of economic dislocation; foreign investors' concern is bottom lines and market share, but Filipino entrepreneurs and managers should recognize that the poor suffer proportionately more, with his warning in Filipino to profiteering traders -- 'Mahiya naman kayo!'

Why he took it upon himself to explain: having served as vice president of the Philippine Chamber of Commerce and Industry and governor of the Management Association of the Philippines, he was immersed in the business community before his appointment

The Rotary frame of the speech: his Rotary Club of Manila presidency, the creed 'Love God, Serve Man' proclaimed at his July 12, 1990 inaugural, its reformulation as 'Justice and Faith' in the Court, and the three memberships he was permitted to retain

The proceedings summarized in five steps: petitioners led by Reps. Garcia, Arroyo, Lagman and Tañada and Sen. Tatad showed the Big Three selling near-identical products at identical prices and moving together; the oil companies and the solicitor general failed to refute this; Article XII, Section 19 forbids monopolies and combinations in restraint of trade; the Court concluded the law sanctioned an oligopoly; and three provisions entrenched it

The three offending provisions: the tariff differential imposing 3 percent on the Big Three's crude imports against 7 percent on new entrants' refined products, worth about twenty centavos a liter; the minimum inventory clause requiring new players to store ten percent of annual sales or a forty-day supply; and the predatory pricing scheme barring sales unreasonably below the industry average cost

The five criticisms he answers: improper intervention in economic policy, failure to hear expert economic advice, the revival of the old ten percent tariff differential, the voiding of the whole law rather than three provisions, and the failure to extend the transition period instead of sending the task back to Congress

First answer: policies called deregulation, liberalization or globalization must conform to the Constitution, and the Decision condemned not deregulation but a law that ran counter to fair competition; the Charter, unlike the 1935, 1973 and 1986 Freedom Constitutions, devotes a full article of 22 sections to economic rights

The American parallel: despite a concise constitution the US Supreme Court struck down laws as oppressive or violative of due process, survived a president's court-packing strategy, and still rules on constitutional issues with an economic dimension

Second answer -- ignorance of the adversarial system: only parties with legal standing may be heard, kibitzers cannot, and editorials, popularity surveys and broadcast commentaries cannot ground decisions, as Justice Hiller B. Zobel said, 'In this country, we do not administer justice by plebiscite'

His illustration from the teachers' cases: in Jacinto v. Court of Appeals the Court unanimously held public schoolteachers had no right to strike, while in Fabella v. Court of Appeals another group won on due process because the investigating committee was illegally composed -- same month, same ponente, opposite outcomes, because each case has its own flesh and blood

Third answer -- the tariff differential: the Court knew that voiding a new law revives the old, but it cannot repeal or modify a law it finds unwise; only Congress may amend and the President may fix tariff rates, and the President had since reset the differential to a uniform 3 percent

Fourth answer -- partial or total unconstitutionality: striking only the three provisions would have cured the barriers to entry but not the cartel itself, leaving the Big Three free to raise pump prices, so the Court left Congress and the President to craft a law free of both flaws

Fifth answer -- partial deregulation: Rep. Enrique Garcia, the prevailing party, argued for keeping deregulation while regulating retail prices through the Energy Regulatory Board; some justices, CJP included, found the plea wise and prudent but bereft of legal underpinnings, since adopting it would have required the Court to legislate, and Tanada v. Angara had already disclaimed review of the wisdom of economic policy

The governing doctrine he draws from Tanada v. Angara, his own unanimously concurred ponencia: the Court will void an economic matter not because it is unwise, improper or inconvenient but only for unconstitutionality or grave abuse of discretion amounting to lack or excess of jurisdiction

The open forum coda: why the Court cannot predetermine the constitutionality of a pending bill, since it is a coequal branch and must not prejudge what litigants may later challenge; his caution that a bill merely dropping the three provisions might still let the Big Three cartelize; and his conclusion that in case of doubt the Court rules in favor of constitutionality, though it had never met a law more constitutionally infirm than RA 8180
signature_phrases: it is simply invalidating a pseudo-deregulation law which in reality restrains free trade and perpetuates a cartel, an oligopoly
The Court is merely upholding constitutional adherence to a truly competitive economy that releases the creative energy of free enterprise.
everyone, rich or poor, must share in the burdens of such economic aberrations
there will come a time when the few who are filled cannot escape the wrath of the many who are hungry
not with a mere wishbone but with a backbone that should neither bend nor break
That justices are not economists or businessmen cannot lessen the cogency or binding effect of their decisions.
Each case has its own flesh and blood and cannot be decided simply on the basis of isolated clinical classroom principles
this Court has no power to pass upon the wisdom, merits and propriety of the acts of its co-equal branches of government
That is separation of powers at work!

stances.claim: The question in the oil case was never whether the Court may fix retail prices or interfere in economics, but whether RA 8180 -- the law letting the oil companies unilaterally set prices -- was constitutional; the Court has the duty, not merely the power, to annul a law that offends the Charter.
stances.rhetorical_move: reframes the accusation by restating the issue, disclaiming any power over the laws of economics as over those of physics or chemistry

stances.claim: Annulling RA 8180 was not a policy statement against deregulation: the Court struck down a pseudo-deregulation law that in reality restrained free trade and perpetuated a cartel, and upheld adherence to a truly competitive economy, leaving Congress to craft a genuine deregulation law.
stances.rhetorical_move: separates the policy from the statute, then hands the task back to the policy-setting branch

stances.claim: The 1987 Constitution uniquely guarantees economic as well as political rights -- a full article of 22 sections unlike the 1935, 1973 and 1986 Charters -- so laws with an economic dimension are not exempt from judicial review, as the US Supreme Court's own history of striking down economic legislation confirms.
stances.rhetorical_move: argues from constitutional text and comparative example, invoking the failed American court-packing episode

stances.claim: The criticism that the Court should have consulted outside economic experts misunderstands the adversarial system: only parties with standing may be heard, and editorials, surveys and commentaries cannot ground a decision, because justice is not administered by plebiscite.
stances.rhetorical_move: corrects a procedural misconception, quotes Justice Zobel, then illustrates with two teachers' cases decided oppositely in the same month by the same ponente

stances.claim: Representative Garcia's plea for partial deregulation, retaining price regulation through the Energy Regulatory Board, was wise and prudent but legally unfounded -- granting it would have required the Court to legislate, a power belonging only to Congress.
stances.rhetorical_move: concedes the merit of the proposal before refusing it on jurisdictional grounds, marking the limits of the Court's own authority

stances.claim: The Court cannot pass upon the constitutionality of a bill before its passage: it is a coequal branch, not an adjunct of Congress or the President, and a judge who prejudges leaves later litigants no chance.
stances.rhetorical_move: answers a question from the open forum with the referee analogy and with the presumption in favor of constitutionality

notable_anecdotes: The big business executive who approached him after the Rotary talk: 'In the past, I severely criticized that Decision. But now, you have given me refreshing parameters and new paradigms in looking at the Supreme Court,' promising to pass the explanation on to the Makati Business Club.

His decision to take the explaining upon himself because, before his appointment, he had been immersed in the business community as vice president of the Philippine Chamber of Commerce and Industry and governor of the Management Association of the Philippines.

The twice-postponed speech: a massive flood cancelled the August 19, 1997 date, he begged off November 12 because the Court was to vote on the Oil Deregulation Law around then, and Bubi Krohn's persistence finally fixed January 6, 1998, during the Court's Christmas break.

His Rotary creed 'Love God, Serve Man,' proclaimed at his July 12, 1990 inaugural as president of the Rotary Club of Manila, reworded in the Court as 'Justice and Faith' and made the title of his new book, a copy of which he presented to the club president.
His Filipino peroration in the Concurring Opinion appealing to wealthy countrymen to stand with the poor in hard times, ending with a rebuke to greedy and heartless traders: 'Mahiya naman kayo!'
His pleasure at the open forum's searching questions running past the usual time, and at the Rotarians who thanked him afterward for the explanation.

The paired teachers' cases decided in the same month by the same ponente -- Jacinto, where striking teachers lost on the right to strike, and Fabella, where teachers won on due process -- offered as proof that each case has its own flesh and blood.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 6 of 'Battles in the Supreme Court' recounted the ruling that big business criticized most during CJP's first three years: Tatad v. Secretary of Energy and its companion case, in which the Court through Justice Puno invalidated RA 8180, the Oil Deregulation Law, by 9 to 2 for allowing Petron, Shell and Caltex to act as an oligopoly and for erecting barriers against new players through its tariff differential, minimum inventory and predatory pricing provisions. CJP reproduced his Concurring Opinion, which insisted that the issue was not whether the Court could fix oil prices but whether a law permitting unilateral pricing was constitutional, that the Court has the duty rather than merely the power to annul such a law, that it was striking a pseudo-deregulation law which perpetuated a cartel rather than opposing deregulation itself, and that in a time of economic dislocation everyone, rich or poor, must share the burden -- ending with an appeal in Filipino to wealthy countrymen and a rebuke to greedy traders. Because he had come from the business community, he took it upon himself to explain the ruling to the Rotary Club of Makati on January 6, 1998, and included that speech in full as a postscript. In it he summarized the proceedings in five steps, listed five criticisms and answered each: economic policy must conform to a Charter that uniquely guarantees economic rights; the demand for outside expert advice misunderstands the adversarial system, in which justice is not administered by plebiscite; the Court knew that voiding a new law revives the old but cannot itself amend; striking only three provisions would have left the cartel intact; and partial deregulation, though wise, would have required the Court to legislate. He closed with the doctrine from his own Tanada v. Angara that only unconstitutionality or grave abuse of discretion may void an economic act, and with the reasons the Court cannot prejudge a pending bill.
